title: The Divinity Verses Examined One by One
subtitle: John 1:1, 8:58, 10:30, 20:28, Philippians 2:6-8, Colossians 2:9, and Titus 2:13 — the Greek grammar, the Trinitarian case, and the unitarian case, side by side
summary: Christians cite a small group of New Testament passages as evidence that Jesus is divine. Each deserves its strongest reading. None should be isolated from Jesus's repeated prayers, his distinction between himself and God, or his identification of the Father as the only true God. Islam reads the exalted language as honor given to God's Messiah, not permission to worship him.

seo.metaTitle: The Divinity Verses Examined One by One: John 1:1 to Titus 2:13
seo.metaDescription: Examine the New Testament verses most often cited for Jesus's divinity, the strongest Christian readings, Jesus's own words about God, and the Quranic conclusion.
keywords: John 10:30 I and the Father are one
Thomas my Lord and my God John 20:28

sections.title: Do the New Testament's Divinity Verses Prove That Jesus Is God?
sections.body: Christians cite several New Testament passages as evidence that Jesus is God. Some are strong within their authors' theology; others allow more than one reading. They should be read beside Jesus's statements that the Father is the only true God, is greater than him, and is his God. Islam therefore reads exalted language through Jesus's prophetic identity and keeps worship for God alone.

sections.title: Read the Strongest Verses With the Whole Record
sections.body: John 1:1, John 8:58, John 10:30, John 20:28, Philippians 2, Colossians 2:9, and Titus 2:13 form an important Christian case. Their grammar and context are debated. The key question is whether they overturn Jesus's dependence on God or describe the authority and honor of God's Messiah.

sections.title: Three Questions for Every Passage
sections.body: Three questions help. What does the wording mean in context? Does it identify Jesus with the one God, or describe authority granted by God? Does the reading fit Jesus's prayers and statements of dependence? A sound doctrine should explain the whole pattern, not only its strongest proof texts.

sections.title: John 1:1: The Word Was God
sections.body:
John says that the Word was with God and was God. The Greek wording commonly receives a qualitative sense: the Word has God's nature while remaining distinct from "the God" with whom the Word was.

This is a strong Christian text, but it is the narrator's prologue, not a sentence Jesus spoke. The same Gospel has Jesus call the Father "the only true God" and himself the one sent by Him (John 17:3). Muslims therefore read John 1:1 through biblical agency and wisdom language; "a god" remains a weak minority translation.

sections.title: John 8:58: Before Abraham, 'I Am'
sections.body: Jesus says, "Before Abraham was, I am." Christians hear a claim of preexistence and divine identity. The Greek phrase can also be ordinary self-identification. Muslims therefore read the verse with Jesus’s distinction between himself and the God who sent him.

sections.title: John 10:30: 'I and the Father Are One'
sections.body:
"I and the Father are one" appears in a discussion of protecting Jesus's followers. Christians understand unity of divine power and identity. Muslims note that the Greek word is neuter, not one person. John 17:21-23 uses related language when Jesus prays that the disciples may be one as he and the Father are one.

Jesus then cites Psalm 82:6 and calls himself the one whom the Father sanctified and sent. Some traditional interpreters understand its "gods" as human judges; others read heavenly beings, as the [USCCB notes on Psalm 82](https://bible.usccb.org/bible/psalms/82) explain. John 10 uses the passage to answer a charge of blasphemy. Muslims read Jesus's language of being sent as consistent with a uniquely authorized Messiah. Christians read the argument as supporting his greater status. The disputed identity of Psalm 82's "gods" should not be used as an undisputed proof either way.

sections.title: John 20:28: 'My Lord and My God'
sections.body: Thomas addresses the risen Jesus as "My Lord and my God." Most scholars read both titles as directed to Jesus; the exclamation-only reading is a minority view. It is one of the strongest Christian texts. The same chapter has Jesus say, "I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God" (John 20:17). God's appointed agents could bear elevated language without becoming the one God. Christians reconcile these texts through two natures. Muslims take Jesus's own statement that he has a God as the clearer guide.

sections.title: Philippians 2:6-8: Form, Equality, and Obedience
sections.body: Philippians describes Christ in "the form of God" and as a servant who obeys God. Many scholars read this as a preexistent Christ choosing humility; an influential minority reads it as an Adam comparison. Either way, the passage distinguishes Christ from God and does not record Jesus identifying himself as God. Islam honors his obedience without treating obedience as deity.

sections.title: Colossians 2:9: The Fullness of Deity
sections.body:
Colossians says that "all the fullness of deity" dwells bodily in Christ. Christians reasonably see very high Christology here. Muslims note that Paul prays for believers to be "filled with all the fullness of God" (Ephesians 3:19). Fullness language can describe God's presence and power without making its recipient God.

Colossians alone cannot decide whether the author means identity with God or the full presence of God's gifts and authority in His Messiah. Jesus's dependence and prayer remain part of the evidence.

sections.title: Titus 2:13: God and Savior
sections.body:
Most modern translations render Titus 2:13 as "our great God and Savior, Jesus Christ." Its Greek construction strongly favors both titles referring to Jesus, though a minority argues for two referents: the Father and Jesus.

This is significant evidence for the Pastoral Epistles, but not a saying of Jesus. Critical scholars dispute Pauline authorship of Titus, while traditional Christians defend it. The verse shows early use of divine titles for Jesus; it does not erase the Gospel record of Jesus worshiping and being sent by God.

sections.title: The Quran's Clear Account of Jesus
sections.body:
The Quran defines Jesus clearly. He is God's Messiah, word conveyed to Mary, spirit from Him, and messenger—not a person within God (4:171). His miraculous creation is compared with Adam's (3:59). He calls people to worship "my Lord and your Lord" (5:72), declares himself God's servant and prophet (19:30), and is described with Mary as eating food, showing creaturely dependence (5:75).

These verses provide the revealed framework for Muslims: exalted titles honor God's Messiah, while the distinction between God and His messenger remains clear.

sections.title: Jesus's Own Words About God
sections.body: Jesus calls the Father "the only true God" (John 17:3), says "the Father is greater than I" (John 14:28), and says he can do nothing by himself (John 5:30). Christian theology explains these statements through two natures. Islam reads them as the plain words of a messenger who depends on God.

sections.title: Exalted Language Is Not the Same as Identity
sections.body: The New Testament can use divine titles for God's appointed agents. Elevated language does not by itself settle identity with the Creator. Jesus's prayer, dependence, and worship of God remain central evidence. Islam honors the strongest Christian readings while preserving the distinction between God and His Messiah.

sections.title: Why Tawhid Fits the Whole Pattern
sections.body: The divinity verses support a highly honored Messiah, especially within later Christian theology. Jesus's own worship provides the clearer center: he prays to God, is sent by God, receives authority from God, and calls the Father his God. Islam preserves this language without turning God's messenger into God.

sections.title: Focused Questions
sections.body:
Q: Do these verses prove that Jesus is God?
A: They are important Christian evidence, but their grammar and context are debated. Jesus’s prayers and dependence remain part of the evidence.

Q: How does Islam read them?
A: Islam honors Jesus as Messiah and messenger, while treating his worship of God as the clearer guide.

Q: What does the Quran say?
A: It calls Jesus God’s Messiah, word, spirit, and servant, and directs worship to God alone. The Islamic conclusion is that later titles do not overturn the prophetic distinction between God and His honored messenger.

faq.question: Which of the seven passages has the strongest grammatical case for calling Jesus God outright?
faq.answer: Titus 2:13 is often regarded as the strongest grammatical case. The Granville Sharp construction joins “God” and “Savior” to “Jesus Christ,” though a minority of scholars argues for two referents: the Father and Jesus.

faq.question: Is Colwell’s rule a reliable proof that John 1:1 calls Jesus “God” rather than “a god”?
faq.answer: Not by itself. Colwell's rule concerns the article with predicate nouns; it does not independently establish that theos is definite in John 1:1c. Philip Harner argued that such nouns often function qualitatively. The grammar remains important, but its theological implications are disputed.

faq.question: Is the “I AM” of John 8:58 definitely a claim to be the God of Exodus 3:14?
faq.answer: Many scholars connect it with Exodus 3:14 and the crowd's attempt to stone Jesus. Unitarian and Muslim scholars note that egō eimi can be ordinary Greek self-identification, as in John 9:9, and read the claim as precedence in God's plan. The passage remains contested rather than settled by vocabulary alone.

faq.question: Does the Bible ever call Jesus God directly, in so many words?
faq.answer: John 1:1, John 20:28, and Titus 2:13 are commonly read that way. The same Gospels record Jesus calling the Father 'the only true God' (John 17:3), 'greater than I' (John 14:28), and 'my God' (John 20:17). Islam gives those direct sayings priority.

faq.question: Is the exclamation reading of John 20:28 as strong as the qualitative reading of John 1:1?
faq.answer: No. The qualitative reading of John 1:1 has broad support, though its implications are disputed. Reading Thomas's words in John 20:28 as a mere exclamation is a minority view; most scholars see both titles as addressed to Jesus.

faq.question: Does presenting both readings mean the question of Jesus’s divinity can’t be answered?
faq.answer: No. The texts can be weighed together. Islam gives priority to Jesus's direct statements about the one God who sent him, and the Quran confirms his prophetic identity. Christian readers may disagree, but the evidence permits a clear conclusion.

furtherReading.title: Jesus as God: The New Testament Use of Theos in Reference to Jesus
furtherReading.author: Murray J. Harris
furtherReading.note: The standard technical, mainstream defense of reading theos as applied to Jesus in the New Testament, with detailed treatments of John 1:1, John 20:28, and Titus 2:13.

furtherReading.title: The Climax of the Covenant: Christ and the Law in Pauline Theology
furtherReading.author: N. T. Wright
furtherReading.note: Collects Wright's influential 1986 essay on harpagmos and Philippians 2:5-11, the strongest modern statement of the kenotic, pre-existence reading.

furtherReading.title: Christology in the Making: A New Testament Inquiry into the Origins of the Doctrine of the Incarnation
furtherReading.author: James D. G. Dunn
furtherReading.note: Presents the Adam-Christology reading of Philippians 2 and argues that New Testament belief in Jesus's pre-existence developed within, rather than from the start of, the earliest tradition.

furtherReading.title: The Doctrine of the Trinity: Christianity's Self-Inflicted Wound
furtherReading.author: Anthony F. Buzzard and Charles F. Hunting
furtherReading.note: The fullest modern statement of the Christian unitarian case against the seven passages examined here , offered so readers can weigh its arguments directly.
